This change causes device uptime sensors in the `unifi` integration to reject newly-computed values if they are too similar to the previous state.

This is to mitigate a long-standing bug which leads to the sensor value (a timestamp) intermittently shifting forward or backward by a minute (or so) every few seconds, filling the recorder with noise unless the user disables these entities.

Two observations from recent testing:

1. When a device (or the entire controller) is offline or restarting, the API response lacks the `uptime` key completely and the library we're using returns `0` instead. We've been taking this at face value and changing the sensor as though the device really started 0 seconds ago, causing the timestamp to jump forward to "now" before jumping back to the correct time after the device is online again. I've pushed an update to the `value_fn` in c555b29516c8ef798738c738d16ac99237193a4f so that a zero value is treated as unknown (`None`).
2. When Home Assistant is restarted, this new strategy of comparing against the old value is ineffective because there's initially no old value to compare with (i.e. `native_value` starts out as `None`). This means the sensors will get a new timestamp that is likely off by a few seconds from the value we were preserving before the restart, creating the illusion of a state change (see below). I don't think there's a practical perfect solution here, just wanted to point it out.

![image](https://github.com/home-assistant/core/assets/33672/3491f766-d82c-4674-8d3c-3bada1db1e0d)

If anyone from Ubiquiti is reading this, please just add an `up_since: <ISO Timestamp Here>` field in the device status API response so this can be a million times simpler :slightly_smiling_face:

Yep!

issue_context.title: Unifi Network uptime sensor changes back and forth every few seconds
issue_context.body:
### The problem

In the logbook (recorder) I see events every few seconds for each Unifi Network device that its uptime has changed. 
The uptime changes from (for example) 13:54 to 13:53, and then back to 13:54, and this process repeats itself constantly.
This floods the logbook, as it happens for each device.
I tried to reload the integration, restart the Unifi devices, but nothing helps.

### What version of Home Assistant Core has the issue?

core-2023.10.1

### What was the last working version of Home Assistant Core?

core-2023.9.3

### What type of installation are you running?

Home Assistant OS

### Integration causing the issue

Unifi Network

### Link to integration documentation on our website

https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/unifi/

### Diagnostics information

![image](https://github.com/home-assistant/core/assets/77859037/ccc90c97-ad10-4862-88c6-c5171459d1ef)

> I took a look at the PR that added the uptime sensor, specifically this piece of code:
> 
> ```
> """Calculate the uptime of the device."""
> return (dt_util.now() - timedelta(seconds=device.uptime)).replace(
>     second=0, microsecond=0
> )
> ```
> 
> If the goal is not to take seconds and microseconds into account for 'uptime', wouldn't it be better to 'zero' them for the current time as well? The current calculation is probably causing the flip back and forth between uptime minutes.

I'm not sure this would be enough to solve the problem; The central limitation is that the controller just returns the uptime as an integer number of seconds, but it's hard to repeatedly derive a consistent original timestamp based only on that information due to a combination of (1) request latency, (2) not knowing how well the controller and the HA device's clocks are synchronized, and (3) not being able to control when (within a given clock second) the entity update occurs.

I looked at the `aiounifi` library and at the data served by the controller itself, and it seems uptime only gets provided this way. The most reliable solution might be to compare the newly-calculated value with the sensor's previous state and just discard the new value if they are close enough (i.e. within a second or two). I've started a PR (#108464) with that change and would welcome reviews/help/commentary/testing there.
Its a challenge :)

review_comments: In an earlier draft, this was `value_change_threshold_fn` or `value_noise_threshold_fn` :shrug: There's probably prior art in other core integrations but I didn't spent a ton of effort on digging.

I've been thinking about this problem, wouldn't it be better to store the previous reported uptime value (without conversion) from the controller as that will remove any conversion issue between host time and controller time

If I understand correctly, you mean storing the uptime value (in seconds) as the actual entity value? The problem there is that this is just a constantly-changing integer that would spam the recorder even more than the current bug does.

The core of the problem isn't that the host and controller have different clocks; It's that we received a number of "seconds ago" without knowing how stale that value is (and the staleness is unpredictable).
Sorry, maybe I was unclear, I meant store it for reference, when entity state was last updated what was the raw value

Sorry, I'm not connecting the dots; what does that buy us or how would the logic change? If I'm not mistaken, the fundamentals of the problem don't really change (since the `uptime` returned from the controller API has all of the uncertainty baked into it). The conversion between the `uptime` integer and our native `datetime` isn't contributing much there IMO

IIRC there was some discrepancy in the logic that could trigger a difference in comparison when doing the utcnow - uptime check every 30 seconds due to slight difference in time between systems (as initial version of implementation I thought it was Ok to have it update twice a minute). If relevant diff comparison is done on the uptime value you remove one layer of uncertainty.

I don't think so? Since you'd have to contrast both the previous uptime value _and_ your best approximation of the absolute time when you think the controller computed it, which leaves you with essentially the same amount of information as we're getting here (i.e. that we assume that `async_update_state` is being triggered as soon as possible after the coordinator's API call finishes).

> when doing the utcnow - uptime check every 30 seconds

Not that it changes the rationale, but in my observation we're getting updates from the coordinator once or twice every second (for every adopted Unifi device and the controller itself).
I guess maybe it changes as you now compare on seconds as well, whereas before it was limited to minutes.

Lets make it optional so the value default to None instead, no need to call the lambda every time.

Ignore that, I see you moved the general control out as well.

If I make the default `None`, then the call site in `async_update_state` would now need to change from this:

```python
        # Update the value only if value is considered to have changed relative to its previous state
        if description.value_changed_fn(
            self.native_value, (value := description.value_fn(self.controller, obj))
        ):
            self._attr_native_value = value
```

to something like this (to re-instate the basic `!=` check that needs to be there when this fn isn't overridden):

```python
        # Update the value only if value is considered to have changed relative to its previous state
        new_value = description.value_fn(self.controller, obj)
        if (description.value_changed_fn is not None and description.value_changed_fn(self.native_value, new_value)) or self._attr_native_value != new_value:
            self._attr_native_value = new_value
```

I chose to treat the original `if old != new` condition as the default `value_changed` function to make the execution flow a little simpler. Is the function call performance cost the concern? (I understood this isn't a huge concern in newer versions of Python, but I haven't done benchmarks. We already lean on callables a lot already in entity implementations, so I figured generalizing these concepts would be more idiomatic.)

Not I just hadn't realised you had moved out the general check. It's fine as it is.

I will go through it once more tomorrow night, if nothing else comes out it could be merged then.
Thank you for the review! I'll let the latest revision run in my dev container for a while to watch how it holds up.
Should I change the library to report None rather than 0?
I think that would make sense, at least for other potential consumers. Would probably need to tag a new major version because of the BC break though
Probably no other primary uses. The library is built for the integration
